title: Arrays
summary: Index access is O(1); a middle insert shifts the tail.

parts.rule: Reach index i in constant time because cells sit in one contiguous block. Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts every later cell, so that costs linear time. Append is amortized constant when the buffer doubles on growth; a single resize is linear.
parts.why: Interview prompts often hide a middle insert inside an innocent-looking "update the list" requirement. If you pick an array and then shift on every insert, your answer quietly becomes O(n) per write. Saying the shift cost out loud before coding stops you from claiming constant time you do not have.
parts.example: Start with the dynamic array [10, 20, 30, 40] that has capacity 4. Read index 2: that is address base+2, value 30, one probe. Now insert 25 at index 1. Shift the tail right: position 3 gets 40, position 2 gets 30, then write 25 at index 1. The array is now [10, 25, 20, 30, 40] and three cells moved. Next append 50 when capacity is full: allocate a new block of size 8, copy five values, then write 50. That append paid a linear copy once; the next few appends are cheap again, which is why we call append amortized O(1). Delete index 1 (25): shift [20, 30, 40, 50] left one slot. Count the moves: one delete shifted four cells.
parts.use: Use an array when you need random index reads, a compact scan, or a fixed-size buffer. Prefer it for sorted data you will binary-search later. Prefer a dynamic array when most growth happens at the end. Prefer it when cache locality matters more than cheap middle splices.
parts.refuse: Refuse an array when the dominant operation is insert or delete in the middle of a long sequence. Refuse claiming O(1) middle insert. Refuse a fixed-capacity array when the prompt requires unbounded growth and you have not described the resize policy. Refuse treating "list" in the prompt as a linked list without checking whether index access is required.

body:
Rule. Reach index i in constant time because cells sit in one contiguous block. Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts every later cell, so that costs linear time. Append is amortized constant when the buffer doubles on growth; a single resize is linear.

Why it matters. Interview prompts often hide a middle insert inside an innocent-looking "update the list" requirement. If you pick an array and then shift on every insert, your answer quietly becomes O(n) per write. Saying the shift cost out loud before coding stops you from claiming constant time you do not have.

Worked example. Start with the dynamic array [10, 20, 30, 40] that has capacity 4. Read index 2: that is address base+2, value 30, one probe. Now insert 25 at index 1. Shift the tail right: position 3 gets 40, position 2 gets 30, then write 25 at index 1. The array is now [10, 25, 20, 30, 40] and three cells moved. Next append 50 when capacity is full: allocate a new block of size 8, copy five values, then write 50. That append paid a linear copy once; the next few appends are cheap again, which is why we call append amortized O(1). Delete index 1 (25): shift [20, 30, 40, 50] left one slot. Count the moves: one delete shifted four cells.

When to use. Use an array when you need random index reads, a compact scan, or a fixed-size buffer. Prefer it for sorted data you will binary-search later. Prefer a dynamic array when most growth happens at the end. Prefer it when cache locality matters more than cheap middle splices.

When to refuse. Refuse an array when the dominant operation is insert or delete in the middle of a long sequence. Refuse claiming O(1) middle insert. Refuse a fixed-capacity array when the prompt requires unbounded growth and you have not described the resize policy. Refuse treating "list" in the prompt as a linked list without checking whether index access is required.
